issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a 19-year-old male with stalking trauma, body-focused shame is hard to reconcile unless there was physical or sexual assault. With the given trauma type, this item is clinically incongruent and stands out from the other appraisal items, which are otherwise plausible for stalking.

issues.item: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless the stalker was also a trusted person. Because trauma type has already been fixed as stalking and no other node supplies context supporting an intimate or trusted-perpetrator stalking scenario, this item is clinically questionable in this profile.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' can fit only if the stalker was a trusted person, but the profile gives no other items in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies to support an interpersonal-betrayal formulation. Paired with global characterological self-blame, this creates a specific relational-trauma narrative that is not otherwise represented in the self-report.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is not impossible, but it implies the stalker was a trusted close other. The rest of the profile provides no supporting items in Memory, Threat, Triggers, or Strategies, and with no active formulation edges this appraisal stands as an unsupported trauma-specific claim. The other appraisal items ('I have to be on guard all the time', 'The world is a dangerous place') fit stalking more generically, but the betrayal item makes the node less coherent as a standalone set.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: These two items are not negative appraisals in the usual cognitive sense; they describe ongoing threat monitoring/safety behavior rather than evaluative beliefs. With a formulation showing no active edges and only the Negative Appraisals node populated, selecting predominantly hypervigilance/vigilance items makes the node content misaligned with the intended construct.

vignette: Adele is a 19-year-old African American male who works as a UX Designer. He has been experiencing significant distress following an intense stalking incident that occurred six months ago. Adele's trauma began when he noticed someone had been following him for several days, eventually confronting him at his apartment building late one night. The stalker was persistent and made threats, leaving Adele feeling both vulnerable and helpless. Since the event, Adele has experienced a range of symptoms indicative of PTSD, with his Negative Appraisals being particularly prominent. He believes that the world is dangerous and unsafe, which has led to an intense sense of vigilance in his daily life. This pervasive fear influences how he perceives various situations, making it difficult for him to relax even in what should be secure environments. Adele had come to believe that constant vigilance was necessary because you never know what can happen next. He began to avoid certain areas where the stalking took place and found himself checking his surroundings frequently, especially when walking home from work or going out at night. The experience has left him feeling like he must be on high alert at all times, constantly scanning for potential threats. In addition to this heightened vigilance, Adele also experiences self-blame, believing that the stalking happened because of how he acted. He had come to believe that if only he had been more careful or different in his behavior, the incident might not have occurred. This has led him to feel a deep sense of guilt and responsibility for what happened, which further exacerbates his anxiety. The combination of these beliefs has significantly impacted Adele's life as a UX Designer. His heightened state of alertness often carries over into work, where he finds it difficult to fully engage with projects and collaborate effectively with colleagues. He frequently checks the doors and windows at home, even when alone in the office or studio, which distracts him from his tasks. The stalking experience has left Adele feeling isolated and disconnected from others. While he wants to trust people again, the fear of being vulnerable keeps him from forming close relationships. This isolation has been particularly challenging given that his social life is already limited due to his intense focus on work. What frightens Adele most is the possibility of a recurrence of such an event. He worries constantly about whether someone could be watching or following him again, and this fear affects almost every aspect of his daily routine. The trauma has left him feeling trapped in a cycle of constant vigilance and self-doubt. Adele finally decided to seek help when the anxiety began to affect his job performance and personal well-being more significantly. He is most hoping for a way to regain control over his life, to be able to trust others again, and to no longer live in a state of fear. Adele recognizes that his current thoughts and behaviors are not sustainable and wants to find ways to break the cycle of constant vigilance and self-blame. The impact of the traumatic event on Adele’s daily life is clear: he has developed a pervasive sense of danger, which drives his vigilant behavior and contributes to feelings of guilt. While these symptoms have been debilitating, Adele's desire for change and hope for recovery are evident in his decision to seek professional help.
